title: Chemical bonding
objectives: Define electronegativity, explain the factors that affect it and its trends, and use electronegativity differences to predict ionic or covalent bonding
Define and describe ionic bonding (NaCl, MgO, CaF₂) and metallic bonding
Define covalent and coordinate (dative covalent) bonding, including expanded octets (SO₂, PCl₅, SF₆), NH₄⁺ and Al₂Cl₆
Describe σ and π bonds in terms of orbital overlap, and use sp, sp² and sp³ hybridisation
Define bond energy and bond length, and use them to compare the reactivity of covalent molecules
Use VSEPR theory to state, explain and predict the shapes of and bond angles in molecules and ions
Describe hydrogen bonding and van der Waals’ forces (id-id and pd-pd), bond polarity and dipole moments, and explain the anomalous properties of water
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding, including expanded octets and odd-electron species
prior: Electronic configurations and ionisation energy trends (Chapter 1)
Simple dot-and-cross diagrams for H₂, Cl₂, H₂O and NaCl (IGCSE)
The idea of a lone pair of electrons
why: Bonding explains why substances behave as they do: why water boils at 100 °C but hydrogen sulfide is a gas, why molecules have the shapes they do, and why some bonds react easily. It underpins almost every later chapter, especially states of matter, energetics and all of organic chemistry. Paper 1 usually has four to six bonding questions, and Paper 2 almost always asks for a shape, a dot-and-cross diagram or an explanation of a boiling point.
intro: Atoms join together because a bonded arrangement has lower energy than separate atoms. In this chapter you will meet the three strong bond types (ionic, covalent and metallic), see how electron pairs push each other into definite molecular shapes, and learn the weaker forces that act between molecules and decide melting and boiling points.

blocks.h: The power of an atom to attract electrons to itself (in a covalent bond).
Electronegativity is measured on the Pauling scale. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0); caesium and francium are the least (about 0.8). It has no units.
What makes an atom more electronegative?

items: Larger nuclear charge: more protons attract the bonding pair more strongly.
Smaller atomic radius: the bonding pair is closer to the nucleus.
Less shielding by inner shells and sub-shells: the bonding pair feels more of the nuclear charge.

head: direction
trend
reason
rows: nuclear charge increases; electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding hardly changes and the radius decreases
extra shells: larger radius and more shielding outweigh the increase in nuclear charge

blocks.h: Predicting the type of bond
The difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms decides how evenly the bonding electrons are shared.

blocks.cap: Electronegativity difference and bond type (a guide, not a sharp cut-off)
head: difference
bond type
examples
rows: polar covalent: electrons shared unequally, δ+ and δ− ends
ionic: an electron is effectively transferred

blocks.name: bondtype
blocks.title: Bond-type meter
blocks.h: Pick any two elements from H to Kr. The meter shows their electronegativity difference, the type of bond expected, and which atom carries the δ− charge.
Pauling values are given in the question when you need them. Always quote the difference, then say what it means: “a large difference, so the bonding is ionic”.

blocks.q: Which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic compound?
blocks.why: K (0.82) and Br (2.96) differ by 2.14, a large difference. The other pairs are close in electronegativity and bond covalently.

blocks.h: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (positively charged cations and negatively charged anions).

Ionic bonds form between metals and non-metals with a large electronegativity difference. The metal atoms lose electrons and the non-metal atoms gain them, usually reaching noble-gas configurations. The ions pack into a giant ionic lattice, and the attraction acts in all directions.

blocks.cap: The three examples in the syllabus
head: compound
ions
electron transfer
rows: Na loses 1 e⁻; Cl gains 1 e⁻
Mg loses 2 e⁻; O gains 2 e⁻
Ca loses 2 e⁻; each F gains 1 e⁻

blocks.h: MgO has a much higher melting point (2852 °C) than NaCl (801 °C) because its ions carry double the charge and are smaller, so the electrostatic attraction is far stronger.
The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

In a metal, the outer electrons leave their atoms and move freely through a lattice of positive ions. The more delocalised electrons each atom provides and the smaller the ion, the stronger the metallic bond: aluminium (3 e⁻ per atom) melts at 660 °C, sodium (1 e⁻) at only 98 °C.

blocks.wrong: Ionic compounds conduct electricity because they contain charged particles.
blocks.right: They conduct only when molten or dissolved, when the ions are free to move. In the solid, the ions are held in fixed positions.

blocks.h: The electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and a shared pair of electrons.
Single, double and triple bonds share one, two and three pairs. You should be able to describe the bonding in H₂, O₂ (O=O), N₂ (N≡N), Cl₂, HCl, CO₂ (O=C=O), NH₃, CH₄, C₂H₆ and C₂H₄.
Expanding the octet

Elements in Period 3 and below have empty d orbitals in their outer shell, so they can have more than eight electrons around them. Examples: SO₂ (S has 10 outer electrons in the structure O=S=O with a lone pair), PCl₅ (10 electrons around P) and SF₆ (12 around S). Period 2 elements such as N and O can never exceed eight.
A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom.

The donor atom must have a lone pair; the acceptor must have an empty orbital. It is drawn as an arrow from donor to acceptor. Once formed, a dative bond is identical to any other covalent bond between the same two atoms.

items: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄⁺Cl⁻: the N lone pair forms a dative bond to H⁺. NH₄⁺ has four identical N–H bonds.

Al₂Cl₆: AlCl₃ has only six outer electrons around Al. A lone pair on a Cl atom of one AlCl₃ forms a dative bond to the Al of another, twice, giving the dimer Al₂Cl₆ (found in the vapour and in the solid at room temperature).

blocks.alt: The ammonium ion: nitrogen bonded to four hydrogens, one bond drawn as an arrow from N to H showing the dative bond
blocks.cap: In NH₄⁺, one N–H bond is formed by donation of the nitrogen lone pair. All four bonds are then identical.

σ and π bonds

items: A σ (sigma) bond forms by direct, end-on overlap of orbitals between the two nuclei. Every single bond is a σ bond.
A π (pi) bond forms by sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals, above and below the σ bond.
A double bond = 1 σ + 1 π. A triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π.

blocks.alt: Left: two orbitals overlapping head-on along the axis between nuclei, labelled sigma. Right: two p orbitals side by side overlapping above and below the axis, labelled pi.
blocks.cap: σ: electron density on the line between the nuclei. π: electron density above and below it, so it is more exposed and weaker.

Hybridisation
To explain the shapes of molecules, the s and p orbitals of an atom are mixed (hybridised) to make new, equal orbitals.

orbitals mixed
shape and angle

blocks.h: Quick rule for carbon: four single bonds → sp³; one double bond → sp²; a triple bond or two double bonds (as in O=C=O or C=C=C) → sp.

blocks.q: Ethanenitrile is CH₃–C≡N. State the number of σ and π bonds and the hybridisation of each carbon atom.
steps: π bonds: the triple bond has 2
CH₃ carbon: four single bonds → sp³; C≡N carbon: triple bond → sp
blocks.err: Counting a triple bond as three σ bonds. Only one bond between any two atoms can be σ.

blocks.h: Bond energy and bond length
The energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state.
The internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms.

Shorter bonds are generally stronger. A π bond is weaker than a σ bond, which is why alkenes (C=C) react much more readily than alkanes. Down Group 17, H–X bonds get longer and weaker (H–F 562, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹), so HI decomposes most easily. N≡N (945 kJ mol⁻¹) is very strong, which is one reason why nitrogen is so unreactive.

Valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory: pairs of electrons around a central atom repel each other and move as far apart as possible. The shape depends on the number of electron pairs, and lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
repulsion: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair
Each lone pair squeezes the bond angle by about 2.5°. For VSEPR, a double or triple bond counts as one region of electron density.

blocks.name: vsepr
blocks.title: VSEPR shape explorer
blocks.h: Choose the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs, or pick a molecule. The 3D model shows the shape, the name and the bond angle. Drag the model to rotate it.
Predicting a shape: the method

items: Count the outer electrons on the central atom.
Add one for each atom bonded by a single bond (each contributes one electron); for an ion, add one electron per negative charge or take one away per positive charge.
Divide by 2 to get the number of pairs; bonding pairs = number of atoms attached; the rest are lone pairs.
Read the shape and angle from the table, then adjust for lone pairs.

blocks.q: Predict the shape of, and bond angle in, the PCl₄⁺ ion.
steps: P has 5 outer electrons; 4 Cl add 4; the + charge removes 1 → 8 electrons = 4 pairs
4 atoms attached → 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs
blocks.err: Forgetting to remove one electron for the positive charge, which gives 4.5 pairs.

blocks.q: Predict the shape of and bond angle in the H₃O⁺ ion.
steps: O has 6 outer electrons; 3 H add 3; the + charge removes 1 → 8 electrons = 4 pairs
blocks.err: Calling it trigonal planar: the lone pair still occupies a position.

blocks.wrong: Water is linear because it has two bonds, like CO₂.
blocks.right: Oxygen in water also has two lone pairs: four pairs in total. The shape is non-linear (bent), 104.5°. CO₂ has no lone pairs on carbon and two double bonds, so it is linear.

blocks.q: What is the shape of the BF₄⁻ ion?
blocks.why: B: 3 + 4 (from F) + 1 (charge) = 8 electrons = 4 bonding pairs, no lone pairs → tetrahedral, 109.5°.

blocks.h: Intermolecular forces act between molecules. They are much weaker than ionic, covalent and metallic bonds, and they decide the melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances. When a simple molecular substance boils, the intermolecular forces are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken.
Bond polarity and dipole moments

In a bond between atoms of different electronegativity, the more electronegative atom gets a partial negative charge (δ−). The bond is polar. A molecule has an overall dipole moment only if its bond dipoles do not cancel: symmetrical molecules such as CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, CCl₄ and SF₆ have polar bonds but no overall dipole. H₂O, NH₃, HCl and CHCl₃ are polar molecules.
The intermolecular forces between molecular entities other than those due to bond formation. A generic term for all intermolecular forces.

Why water is unusual

items: High melting and boiling points: each H₂O can form up to four hydrogen bonds (two through its H atoms, two through its lone pairs). H₂O boils at 100 °C, whereas H₂S, with more electrons, boils at −60 °C.
High surface tension: hydrogen bonds pull surface molecules strongly inwards.
Ice is less dense than liquid water: in ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open hexagonal lattice with more space than in the liquid, so ice floats.

blocks.title: Boiling points of the Group 16 hydrides

blocks.h: From H₂S to H₂Te the boiling point rises because the number of electrons increases, so id-id forces get stronger. H₂O breaks the trend because of hydrogen bonding.

blocks.name: imf
blocks.title: Intermolecular forces sorter
blocks.h: For each substance, tick every intermolecular force it has. Then check your answer and see the explanation.
In general, ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are stronger than intermolecular forces, which is why giant structures have much higher melting points than simple molecular substances.

blocks.wrong: When water boils, the O–H bonds break.
blocks.right: Boiling separates whole H₂O molecules by overcoming the hydrogen bonds between them. The O–H covalent bonds stay intact; steam is still H₂O.

items: Every molecule that contains oxygen and hydrogen forms hydrogen bonds.
The H must be bonded directly to N, O or F. Methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, contains O and H but has no O–H bond, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself.
Tetrachloromethane has polar bonds but no overall dipole moment.
The four C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel.
Id-id forces are present between all molecules.
Every molecule has electrons that can form temporary dipoles.

blocks.h: Dot-and-cross diagrams show the outer-shell electrons, with dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for another. Show lone pairs as well as bonding pairs.

items: Ionic: draw separate ions in square brackets with their charges, e.g. [Na]⁺ [Cl with 8 electrons]⁻. Do not draw a shared pair.
Covalent: draw the shared pairs in the overlap between atoms; a double bond has two pairs (four electrons) in the overlap.
Coordinate: the shared pair has two electrons of the same symbol (both dots or both crosses) because they came from one atom.
Expanded octets: in SF₆, six S–F shared pairs give sulfur 12 outer electrons. In PCl₅, phosphorus has 10.
Odd-electron species (free radicals), such as NO or a chlorine atom, have one unpaired electron.

blocks.q: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of a carbon monoxide molecule, CO.
blocks.a: C and O share three pairs: two pairs made from one electron of each atom, plus one dative pair donated by oxygen (both electrons shown as oxygen's symbol). Each atom also keeps one lone pair. Both atoms then have 8 outer electrons.

blocks.h: Count electrons when you finish: every electron from the original atoms (plus or minus the ion charge) must appear exactly once.

summary: Electronegativity: power of an atom to attract electrons to itself. Increases across a period, decreases down a group (nuclear charge, radius, shielding).
Large electronegativity difference → ionic; small → polar covalent; zero → non-polar covalent.
Ionic bonding: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Metallic: between positive ions and delocalised electrons.
Covalent bond: attraction between two nuclei and a shared pair. Dative bond: both electrons from one atom (NH₄⁺, Al₂Cl₆, H₃O⁺).
Period 3 elements can expand the octet (SO₂, PCl₅, SF₆).
σ = end-on overlap; π = sideways overlap of p orbitals. Double = σ + π; triple = σ + 2π.
sp³ 109.5°, sp² 120° (one π possible), sp 180° (two π possible).
VSEPR: pairs repel and get as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more and reduce bond angles by about 2.5° each.
Shapes: linear 180°, trigonal planar 120°, tetrahedral 109.5°, pyramidal 107°, bent 104.5°, trigonal bipyramidal 90°/120°, octahedral 90°.
van der Waals' forces: id-id (all molecules; more electrons → stronger), pd-pd (polar molecules), hydrogen bonds (N–H, O–H, H–F to a lone pair on N, O or F).
Symmetrical molecules with polar bonds can have no overall dipole (CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄).
Hydrogen bonding explains the high boiling point and surface tension of water and why ice floats.
Strong bonds (ionic, covalent, metallic) are stronger than intermolecular forces.

practice.q: Use electronegativity values (Li 1.0, F 4.0, C 2.6, Cl 3.2) to predict the bonding in LiF and CCl₄.
practice.a: LiF: difference 3.0 → ionic. CCl₄: difference 0.6 → polar covalent bonds, but the molecule is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so it has no overall dipole.

practice.q: Predict the shape of, and bond angle in, the AsF₆⁻ ion.
practice.a: As 5 + 6 + 1 (charge) = 12 electrons = 6 bonding pairs, no lone pairs → octahedral, 90°.

practice.q: Explain why the bond angle in NF₃ is smaller than the bond angle in BF₃.
practice.a: BF₃: 3 bonding pairs, no lone pair → trigonal planar, 120°. NF₃: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair; the lone pair repels more strongly → pyramidal, about 107°.

practice.q: State the number of σ and π bonds in propenenitrile, CH₂=CH–C≡N.
Explain why ethanol (M<sub>r</sub> 46) boils at 78 °C but propane (M<sub>r</sub> 44) boils at −42 °C.
practice.a: Ethanol has an O–H group, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which need much more energy to overcome. Propane has only id-id forces of similar strength (similar number of electrons).

practice.q: Describe how a coordinate bond forms when NH₃ reacts with BF₃.
practice.a: The lone pair on N is donated into the empty orbital on B (which has only 6 outer electrons). Both electrons in the new N→B bond come from nitrogen.

assessment.q: Which correctly describes the trend in electronegativity?
o: is the same for all halogens
assessment.why: Across a period, nuclear charge rises while shielding stays similar and the radius falls.

assessment.q: Which substance contains a coordinate bond?
assessment.why: NH₄⁺ forms when the N lone pair of NH₃ is donated to H⁺.

assessment.q: How many σ bonds and π bonds are there in ethyne, HC≡CH?
assessment.why: 2 C–H σ + 1 σ in C≡C = 3 σ; the triple bond has 2 π.

assessment.q: What is the shape of a molecule of PCl₃?
assessment.why: 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on P → pyramidal, about 107°.

assessment.q: Which molecule has an overall dipole moment?
assessment.why: In CHCl₃ the C–H and C–Cl dipoles do not cancel. The others are symmetrical.

assessment.q: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene?
assessment.why: Three regions of electron density (two C–H and one C=C) → sp², 120°.

assessment.q: Which liquid has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
assessment.why: Methylamine has N–H bonds and a lone pair on N.

assessment.q: Which explains why the boiling points of the noble gases increase down the group?
o: more electrons, so stronger id-id forces
assessment.why: Noble gases are single atoms with only id-id forces, which increase with the number of electrons.

assessment.q: What is the F–S–F bond angle in SF₆?
assessment.why: Octahedral: adjacent bonds are at 90° (opposite bonds at 180°).

assessment.q: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
o: hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open lattice
covalent bonds are longer in ice
assessment.why: The hydrogen-bonded lattice in ice has more space between molecules than the liquid.

assessment.q: Which compound has the largest electronegativity difference between its elements?
The bond angle in H₂O is smaller than in NH₃ because…
o: O is more electronegative than N
H₂O has two lone pairs, which repel more
assessment.why: Two lone pairs (H₂O) compress the bond angle more than one (NH₃): 104.5° vs 107°.

assessment_s.q:
This question is about boron trichloride, BCl₃, and the ion BCl₄⁻.
(a) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for BCl₃, showing outer electrons only. [1]
(b) State the shape of BCl₃ and the Cl–B–Cl bond angle. [2]
(c) BCl₃ reacts with Cl⁻ to form BCl₄⁻. Name the type of bond formed and state the new bond angle. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) B in the centre sharing one pair with each Cl (one dot + one cross); each Cl has 3 lone pairs; B has 6 outer electrons and no lone pair.
(b) trigonal planar; 120°
(c) coordinate (dative covalent) bond, from a lone pair on Cl⁻ to the empty orbital on B; tetrahedral, 109.5°

assessment_s.q:
The boiling points of three compounds are given: CH₄ −162 °C, SiH₄ −112 °C, NH₃ −33 °C.
(a) Name the strongest type of intermolecular force in CH₄ and in NH₃. [2]
(b) Explain why SiH₄ has a higher boiling point than CH₄. [2]
(c) Draw a diagram showing one hydrogen bond between two NH₃ molecules. Include partial charges and lone pairs. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) CH₄: id-id (London) forces; NH₃: hydrogen bonds
(b) SiH₄ has more electrons (18 vs 10), so its id-id forces are stronger and need more energy to overcome.
(c) N–H (δ+ on H) of one molecule lined up with the lone pair on N (δ−) of another, shown as a dashed line, N–H···N close to 180°.

opts: Both electronegativity and first ionisation energy increase at every step from Mg to P.

pp.mis: Calling every bond with an electronegative atom ionic
pp.stem: Elements P, Q and R have Pauling electronegativities of 0.9, 2.5 and 3.0. Which statement about the substances PR, QR and R₂ is correct?
pp.exp: PR: difference 2.1, large → ionic. QR: difference 0.5 → polar covalent. R₂: difference 0 → non-polar covalent.

pp.skill: Properties of bonding types
pp.mis: Thinking ionic solids conduct because they contain ions
pp.stem: Which statement about the properties linked to different types of bonding is correct?
opts: All covalent substances have low melting points.
Metals conduct electricity as solids because of delocalised electrons, but ionic solids do not conduct.
Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the solid state because they contain ions.
Every molecule that contains both nitrogen and hydrogen forms hydrogen bonds.
pp.exp: Delocalised electrons move through a solid metal. In an ionic solid the ions are fixed, so it conducts only when molten or in solution. Giant covalent substances such as diamond have very high melting points, and hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F.

pp.skill: Identifying ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding together
pp.mis: Forgetting the dative bonds in NH₄⁺ and in nitrate
pp.stem: In which of these solids would you find ions and covalent bonds, yet no dative covalent bond anywhere?
pp.exp: NaOH: ionic between Na⁺ and OH⁻; covalent O–H in the hydroxide ion; no dative bond. NH₄NO₃ has a dative bond in NH₄⁺ (and in the nitrate ion). CaCl₂ is ionic only. Al₂Cl₆ is covalent with dative bonds.

pp.skill: Recognising dative covalent bonding
pp.mis: Thinking an ion must contain ionic bonds
pp.stem: Which types of bonding are present in the oxonium ion, H₃O⁺?
pp.exp: H₃O⁺ forms when a lone pair on the oxygen of H₂O is donated to H⁺. It has two ordinary O–H covalent bonds and one dative bond (identical once formed). There is no ionic bonding within the ion itself.

pp.skill: Dot-and-cross diagram of a dative bond
pp.mis: Thinking the acceptor keeps an incomplete shell
pp.stem: Ammonia reacts with boron trifluoride to form H₃N–BF₃. Which statement about the dot-and-cross diagram of H₃N–BF₃ is correct?
opts: Boron has only six outer electrons.
Both electrons in the N–B bond come from the nitrogen atom.
Nitrogen still has one lone pair.
Boron has an expanded octet of ten electrons.
pp.exp: The lone pair on N is donated into the empty orbital on B, forming a dative bond. B now has eight outer electrons; N has used its lone pair, so it has none left.

pp.skill: Type of bond formed by a lone pair
pp.mis: Confusing a dative bond with an intermolecular force
pp.stem: Ammonia molecules react with silver ions to form [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. What type of bond forms between each nitrogen atom and the silver ion?
pp.exp: Each N donates its lone pair to an empty orbital on Ag⁺, forming a coordinate (dative covalent) bond.

pp.skill: Counting dative and π bonds in an ionic compound
pp.mis: Missing the dative bond in each NH₄⁺
pp.stem: How many coordinate bonds and how many π bonds are there in one formula unit of ammonium carbonate, (NH₄)₂CO₃? (Treat the carbonate ion as having one C=O double bond.)
pp.exp: Each of the two NH₄⁺ ions contains one dative N–H bond → 2. The carbonate ion has one C=O → 1 π bond.

pp.skill: Counting σ and π bonds
pp.mis: Counting a double bond as two σ bonds
pp.stem: How many σ bonds and π bonds are there in a molecule of propenal, CH₂=CH–CHO?
pp.exp: σ: 4 C–H + 1 C=C (σ part) + 1 C–C + 1 C=O (σ part) = 7. π: one in C=C and one in C=O = 2.

pp.skill: σ bonds and hybridisation in a nitrile
pp.mis: Giving the CH₃ carbon sp²
pp.stem: Ethanenitrile has the structure CH₃–C≡N. Which row is correct?
pp.exp: σ bonds: 3 C–H + 1 C–C + 1 in C≡N = 5. The CH₃ carbon has four single bonds (sp³); the nitrile carbon has a triple bond (sp).

pp.skill: Counting sp³ orbitals used in bonding
pp.mis: Counting sp³ carbons instead of orbitals
pp.stem: Pent-2-ene is CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃. Counting every carbon atom in the molecule, how many sp³ hybrid orbitals take part in bonding altogether?
pp.exp: C1, C4 and C5 are sp³ (only single bonds); C2 and C3 are sp². Each sp³ carbon uses four sp³ orbitals: 3 × 4 = 12.

pp.skill: sp² carbons in a cumulated diene
pp.mis: Calling the central allene carbon sp²
pp.stem: Penta-1,2-diene is CH₂=C=CH–CH₂–CH₃. In one molecule, how many carbon atoms use sp² hybrid orbitals?
pp.exp: C1 and C3 each have one double bond → sp². C2 has two double bonds → sp (linear). C4 and C5 are sp³.

pp.skill: Counting sp² carbons
pp.mis: Including the CH₃ carbon
pp.stem: Isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene) is CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH₂. How many of its carbon atoms are sp² hybridised?
pp.exp: The four carbons in the two C=C bonds are sp². The CH₃ carbon is sp³.

pp.skill: Hybridisation in a molecule with double and triple bonds
pp.mis: Forgetting that a triple bond means sp
pp.stem: But-1-en-3-yne is CH₂=CH–C≡CH. Which hybridisation states occur among its four carbons?
pp.exp: The two C=C carbons are sp²; the two C≡C carbons are sp. There is no carbon with only single bonds, so no sp³.

pp.skill: Orbital overlaps in ethene
pp.mis: Forgetting the s–sp² overlap in C–H bonds
pp.stem:
Consider these four overlaps:
1 p with p (sideways)
2 sp² with sp²
3 s with sp²
4 s with s
Which of them occur in an ethene molecule, H₂C=CH₂?
pp.exp: C=C: σ from sp²–sp² (2) and π from p–p (1). Each C–H: H 1s with C sp² (3). There is no H–H bond, so no s–s overlap.

pp.skill: Orbital overlaps in carbon dioxide
pp.mis: Assuming both atoms in a bond have the same hybridisation
pp.stem:
In CO₂, carbon is sp hybridised and each oxygen is sp² hybridised. Consider these four overlaps:
1 p with p (sideways)
2 sp with sp²
3 s with sp
4 sp with sp
Which of them occur in CO₂?
pp.exp: Each C=O: σ from C sp with O sp² (2) and π from p–p sideways overlap (1). There are no H atoms (no s orbitals in bonding) and no C–C bond (no sp–sp).

pp.skill: σ and π overlap in an sp molecule
pp.mis: Thinking π bonds come from hybrid orbitals
pp.stem: In ethyne, H–C≡C–H, each carbon atom is sp hybridised. Which row describes how a C–H σ bond and the π bonds are formed?
pp.exp: C–H σ: H 1s overlaps a C sp orbital. The two π bonds come from sideways overlap of the two unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon.

pp.skill: Planarity and σ-bond count
pp.mis: Thinking every atom in a molecule with C=O lies in one plane
pp.stem:
Consider two claims about propanone, CH₃COCH₃.
Claim 1: every atom in the molecule lies in one flat plane.
Claim 2: the molecule has nine σ bonds.
Which claims are true?
pp.exp: σ bonds: 6 C–H + 2 C–C + 1 in C=O = 9. The CH₃ carbons are tetrahedral (sp³), so their H atoms cannot all lie in the plane of the C=O group.

pp.skill: σ/π bonds and ring planarity
pp.mis: Assuming all six-membered rings are flat
pp.stem:
Cyclohexene, C₆H₁₀, has one C=C bond in its ring. Four claims about it are listed.
1 Every bond in the molecule is a σ bond.
2 The molecule has at least one π bond.
3 All six ring carbons lie in one flat plane.
4 The ring is puckered rather than flat.
Which two claims are true?
pp.exp: The C=C bond contains a π bond. Four of the ring carbons are sp³ (tetrahedral), so the ring is puckered, not flat. (Benzene is flat because all six carbons are sp².)

pp.skill: Shape and σ-bond count of a ring
pp.mis: Counting only the C–C bonds
pp.stem: Which row describes a benzene molecule, C₆H₆?
pp.exp: Every carbon is sp² (trigonal planar), so the molecule is planar. σ bonds: 6 C–C + 6 C–H = 12.

pp.skill: VSEPR shape from electron pairs
pp.mis: Ignoring lone pairs when naming the shape
pp.stem: Which row matches the electron pairs around a central atom with the correct molecular shape?
pp.exp: 2 bonding + 1 lone pair → three regions arranged trigonally, so the atoms form a non-linear (bent) shape (about 118°), as in SO₂. 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs is trigonal planar; 4 + 2 is square planar; 4 + 0 is tetrahedral.

pp.skill: Shape of an ion with a lone pair
pp.mis: Ignoring the lone pair on the central atom
pp.stem: The nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, has one N=O bond, one N–O bond and one lone pair on the nitrogen atom. What is its shape?
pp.exp: Three regions of electron density around N (two bonds and a lone pair) → trigonal arrangement; with only two atoms attached, the shape is non-linear (bent), about 117°.

pp.skill: Bond angle in a protonated species
pp.mis: Using the angle of the neutral molecule
pp.stem: The oxonium ion, H₃O⁺, forms when a water molecule accepts a proton. Predict the H–O–H angle in H₃O⁺.
pp.exp: O has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair → pyramidal, about 107°, the same as NH₃.

pp.skill: Electron-pair arrangement before and after dative bonding
pp.mis: Forgetting that the extra pair changes the arrangement
pp.stem: Boron trifluoride, BF₃, reacts with a fluoride ion to form BF₄⁻. What is the arrangement of the bonding pairs around boron in each species?
pp.exp: BF₃: three bonding pairs, no lone pair → trigonal planar. BF₄⁻: the F⁻ lone pair forms a dative bond, giving four bonding pairs → tetrahedral.

pp.skill: Molecules with more than one bond angle
pp.mis: Thinking octahedral molecules have two angles
pp.stem:
Which molecules have more than one bond angle? (Ignore angles of 180°.)
1 BCl₃
2 PCl₅
3 SF₆
pp.exp: PCl₅ (trigonal bipyramidal) has 120° and 90°. BCl₃ has only 120°. SF₆ has only 90° (besides 180°).

pp.skill: Same shape and lone pairs
pp.mis: Matching species by number of atoms only
pp.stem: In which pair do both species have the same shape and the same number of lone pairs on the central atom?
pp.exp: BF₄⁻ and CH₄ are both tetrahedral with no lone pair on the central atom. H₂O is bent and CO₂ linear; NH₃ is pyramidal and BF₃ trigonal planar; SO₂ is bent.

pp.skill: Ranking bond angles
pp.mis: Forgetting the effect of lone pairs
pp.stem: Which row lists the bond angles from smallest to largest?
pp.exp: H₂O 104.5° (two lone pairs) < CH₄ 109.5° < CO₂ 180°.

pp.skill: Comparing bond angles between species
pp.mis: Forgetting the 90° angles in trigonal bipyramidal molecules
pp.stem: In which pair does the first species have a narrower bond angle than any bond angle in the second species?

pp.skill: Smallest bond angle
pp.mis: Ranking by size of atoms rather than electron pairs
pp.stem: Which of these species would VSEPR theory predict to have the narrowest bond angle?
pp.exp: H₂S has two lone pairs on S, like H₂O → bent, under 104.5°. PCl₃ has one lone pair (about 107°), NH₄⁺ none (109.5°), BF₃ is planar (120°).

pp.skill: Facts about an octahedral molecule
pp.mis: Thinking polar bonds always make a polar molecule
pp.stem: Which statement about a molecule of sulfur hexafluoride, SF₆, is correct?
opts: The molecule has bond angles of 90° and 120°.
The sulfur atom has no lone pair of electrons.
The molecule has an overall dipole moment.
The shape of the molecule is trigonal bipyramidal.
pp.exp: S uses all six outer electrons to bond to six F atoms: six bonding pairs, no lone pairs → octahedral, 90°. The six S–F dipoles cancel, so there is no overall dipole.

pp.skill: Counting bond pairs and lone pairs
pp.mis: Forgetting lone pairs on outer atoms or ions
pp.stem: Which row correctly counts the bonding pairs and lone pairs in the species named?
pp.exp: H₂O: 2 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs on O. H₃O⁺: 3 bond pairs, 1 lone pair. CH₄: 4 and 0. F⁻: 0 bond pairs and 4 lone pairs.

pp.skill: Properties of the oxonium ion
pp.mis: Thinking a dative bond stays different after it forms
pp.stem: Which statement about the oxonium ion, H₃O⁺, is correct?
opts: All the H–O–H bond angles are 109.5°.
It contains one dative O–H bond that is weaker than the other two O–H bonds.
The oxygen atom has one lone pair.
It acts as a base by accepting H⁺.
pp.exp: O: 6 + 3 − 1 = 8 electrons = 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair (pyramidal, about 107°). All three O–H bonds are identical once formed. H₃O⁺ is an acid (it donates H⁺).

pp.skill: Deducing charge and lone pairs from a bond angle
pp.mis: Not linking the bond angle to the number of lone pairs
pp.stem: An ion contains one oxygen atom and three hydrogen atoms. Its H–O–H bond angle is approximately 107°. Which row is correct?
pp.exp: 107° means pyramidal: 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair = 4 pairs = 8 electrons. O (6) + 3 H (3) = 9, so one electron has been removed: charge +1. This is H₃O⁺.

pp.skill: Bond angle changes on forming dative bonds
pp.mis: Thinking adding a bond always opens up the angle
pp.stem:
Two reactions are shown.
1 BCl₃ + Cl⁻ → BCl₄⁻
2 H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺
How does the bond angle around the central atom change in each reaction?
pp.exp: 1: trigonal planar 120° → tetrahedral 109.5°, a decrease. 2: H₂O 104.5° (two lone pairs) → H₃O⁺ 107° (one lone pair), an increase.

pp.skill: Shape changes in a proton-transfer reaction
pp.mis: Mixing up which species is the acid
pp.stem: Consider the reaction H₃O⁺ + NH₃ → H₂O + NH₄⁺. Which statement is correct?
opts: The H–O–H bond angle decreases from about 107° to 104.5°.
A hydrogen bond forms between N and H.
pp.exp: H₃O⁺ (pyramidal, 107°) becomes H₂O (bent, 104.5°). NH₃ (107°) becomes NH₄⁺ (109.5°), an increase. NH₃ accepts H⁺, so it is a base, and the new N–H bond is a dative covalent bond, not a hydrogen bond.

pp.skill: Ordering bond angles in a larger molecule
pp.mis: Treating every angle at an sp³ atom as 109.5°
pp.stem:
In methoxyethene, CH₃–O–CH=CH₂, three bond angles are considered:
x = the C–O–C angle
y = an H–C–H angle in the CH₃ group
z = the C=C–H angle
Which row lists them from smallest to largest?
pp.exp: x: O has 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs → about 104.5°. y: tetrahedral carbon → 109.5°. z: sp² carbon → 120°.

pp.skill: Bond angles at atoms with lone pairs
pp.mis: Forgetting the lone pair on nitrogen
pp.stem:
Methyl nitrite has the structure CH₃–O–N=O. Three angles are labelled:
1 an H–C–H angle
2 the C–O–N angle
3 the O–N=O angle (N has one lone pair)
What is the order of these angles, smallest first?
pp.exp: 2: O has 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs → about 104.5°. 1: tetrahedral C → 109.5°. 3: N has 3 regions (2 bonds + 1 lone pair) → about 117°, a little under 120°.

pp.skill: Ordering bond angles including a linear group
pp.mis: Forgetting that a triple-bonded carbon is linear
pp.stem:
In the molecule CH₃–NH–CH₂–C≡N, three angles are considered:
x = the C–N–C angle
y = the C–C≡N angle
z = an H–C–H angle in the CH₃ group
What is the order of decreasing size?
pp.exp: y: sp carbon → 180°. z: tetrahedral → 109.5°. x: N has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair → about 107°. So y > z > x.

pp.skill: Hydrogen bonding explains a higher boiling point
pp.mis: Thinking boiling breaks covalent bonds
pp.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, boils at −33 °C, but phosphine, PH₃, boils at −88 °C. What is the reason for this difference?
opts: N–H bonds are stronger than P–H bonds.
There is hydrogen bonding between NH₃ molecules but not between PH₃ molecules.
The id-id forces between NH₃ molecules are stronger than those between PH₃ molecules.
Nitrogen has a higher first ionisation energy than phosphorus.
pp.exp: N is small and very electronegative, so NH₃ molecules hydrogen bond. Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. PH₃ has more electrons, so its id-id forces are actually stronger.

pp.skill: Anomalous boiling point in a hydride series
pp.mis: Explaining boiling points with bond strength
pp.stem: The boiling points of the hydrogen halides increase from HCl to HBr to HI, but HF has the highest boiling point of all. Which statement explains why HF does not fit the trend?
opts: Fluorine atoms have fewer electrons, so there is less shielding.
There are strong hydrogen bonds between HF molecules but not between the other hydrogen halide molecules.
The H–F bond is the strongest, so more energy is needed to boil HF.
HF molecules are the smallest, so more of them fit in a given volume.
pp.exp: HF has H bonded to F, which has lone pairs, so HF molecules hydrogen bond. From HCl to HI the boiling point rises because the number of electrons, and so the id-id force, increases.

pp.skill: Hydrogen bonding in isomers
pp.mis: Thinking any molecule with O and H hydrogen bonds
pp.stem: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, and methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, have the same M<sub>r</sub>. Ethanol boils at 78 °C, methoxymethane at −24 °C. Which statement explains the difference?
opts: The C–O bonds in ethanol are stronger.
Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other; methoxymethane molecules cannot.
Ethanol has more electrons per molecule.
pp.exp: Ethanol has an O–H group. In methoxymethane all the H atoms are bonded to carbon, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself. Both have 26 electrons, and methoxymethane is polar (bent C–O–C).

pp.skill: Polarity and boiling point
pp.mis: Comparing covalent bond strengths to explain boiling points
pp.stem: Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, and butane, C₄H₁₀, both have M<sub>r</sub> = 58. Why does propanone have a higher boiling point?
opts: Propanone molecules are polar, so they have permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces as well as id-id forces.
Propanone molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other.
pp.exp: The C=O bond makes propanone polar, adding pd-pd forces. It has no O–H, so no hydrogen bonding between its molecules; it has 32 electrons, fewer than butane (34).

pp.skill: Substances with only id-id forces
pp.mis: Thinking polar bonds always give pd-pd forces
pp.stem: Which of these liquids is held together only by London (id-id) forces between its molecules?
pp.exp: CCl₄ has polar bonds, but its tetrahedral shape makes it non-polar overall, so only id-id forces act. Propanone has pd-pd forces; methanol and HF hydrogen bond.

pp.skill: Planar and non-polar molecules
pp.mis: Thinking polar bonds always make a polar molecule
pp.stem: Which molecule is planar and has no overall dipole moment?
pp.exp: BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so the B–F dipoles cancel. NH₃ is pyramidal and polar; H₂O is polar; CH₂Cl₂ is tetrahedral (not planar) and polar.

pp.skill: σ and π bonds in an alkene
pp.stem: This question is about the bonding in propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃.

ms: the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and a shared pair of electrons

parts.q: State the hybridisation of each carbon atom in propene.
ms: the two C=C carbons are sp²; the CH₃ carbon is sp³

parts.q: Explain how the σ bond and the π bond in C=C are formed, referring to the orbitals that overlap.
ms: σ: direct (end-on) overlap of an sp² orbital from each carbon, between the nuclei
π: sideways overlap of the unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon, above and below the σ bond

parts.q: Suggest why the π bond, rather than the σ bond, breaks when propene reacts with bromine.
ms: the π bond is weaker / its electron density is above and below the bond axis, more exposed to electrophiles

pp.skill: Dot-and-cross, hybridisation and π bonding in an N=N compound
pp.stem: Diazene, HN=NH, contains a double bond between its two nitrogen atoms.

parts.q: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of diazene, showing outer electrons only.
ms: two shared pairs (one from each N in each pair) between the N atoms; one shared pair between each N and its H
one lone pair on each N; each N has 8 outer electrons

parts.q: Deduce the hybridisation of the nitrogen atoms.
ms: sp² (three regions: N=N, N–H and a lone pair)
about 117–118° (just under 120°, because of the lone pair)

pp.skill: Dative bonding and the shape of a tetrahedral ion
pp.stem: Boron trifluoride, BF₃, reacts with fluoride ions to form the tetrafluoroborate ion, BF₄⁻.

parts.q: Describe how the coordinate (dative covalent) bond forms when BF₄⁻ is made.
ms: a lone pair on F⁻ is donated into the empty orbital on boron (which has only six outer electrons in BF₃)

parts.q: Name the shape of the BF₄⁻ ion and state the F–B–F bond angle.
ms: tetrahedral

parts.q: Explain why all four B–F bonds in BF₄⁻ are the same length.
ms: once formed, a dative bond is identical to the other covalent bonds between the same atoms

pp.skill: VSEPR shape and angle of a bent molecule
pp.stem: Dichlorine oxide, Cl₂O, has the structure Cl–O–Cl, with two lone pairs on the oxygen atom.

parts.q: Name the shape of a Cl₂O molecule predicted by VSEPR theory.
ms: non-linear (bent / V-shaped)

parts.q: Predict the Cl–O–Cl bond angle. Explain your answer.
ms: about 104.5° (accept 104–105°)
four electron pairs (2 bond, 2 lone); lone pairs repel more than bond pairs, so the angle is less than 109.5°

pp.skill: Ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding in one diagram
pp.stem: Methylamine, CH₃NH₂, reacts with hydrogen chloride gas to form the white solid methylammonium chloride, CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

parts.q: Describe a diagram showing all the types of bonding present in methylammonium chloride.
ms: ionic: separate CH₃NH₃⁺ and Cl⁻ ions with charges (Cl⁻ with 8 outer electrons in brackets)
covalent C–H, C–N and N–H shared pairs, and one N–H bond shown as a coordinate bond (arrow from N to H / both electrons from N)

parts.q: State the H–N–H bond angle in the CH₃NH₃⁺ ion.
ms: 109.5° (four bonding pairs, no lone pair on N)

pp.skill: Expanded octet, bond angle, dipoles and id-id forces
pp.stem: This question is about phosphorus pentafluoride, PF₅, and hydrogen sulfide, H₂S.

parts.q: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of PF₅, showing outer electrons only.
ms: five P–F shared pairs (one dot + one cross each); each F has three lone pairs; P has 10 outer electrons and no lone pair

parts.q: Name the shape of a PF₅ molecule.
ms: trigonal bipyramidal

parts.q: H₂S is polar. Predict the H–S–H bond angle using VSEPR theory and explain your answer.
ms: less than 109.5° (about 104.5° by VSEPR; accept 92–105°)
two bonding pairs and two lone pairs on S
lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs

parts.q: Show the bond dipoles in H₂S.
ms: δ+ on each H and δ− on S (S is more electronegative than H)

parts.q: H₂S has 18 electrons per molecule and H₂O has 10. Identify which has the stronger id-id forces and explain why H₂O nevertheless has the higher boiling point.
ms: H₂S has stronger id-id forces because it has more electrons
H₂O forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which are much stronger in total
